Got the game for free and it has been sitting in my backlog for a while. Some while ago I finally decided to clear this game with high expectations seeing it receive a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately I was faced with only disappointment.

At first the gameplay is intriguing and engaging. The terminal style UI certainly looks cool. There are quests that procedurally guide you through the mechanics of the game, and the discovery process keeps the gameplay fresh, but not for long until you join the hacker organization.

From that point what you do is just repeating the same hacking routine again and again, and it gets repetitive very quickly. At this point the only thing left that can do some good for this game is the story. My last hope for the game was that after hours of labour I would uncover traces of a big conspiracy that leads me to something like stopping a skynet, or fighting myself in a moral conflict, you get the meaning.

But no! The main plot is linear and doesn't have much depth to it. It was so uninspiring that I didn't even know I came to the end of the story, just after I did the usual hacking stuff I was greeted with a voice recording and I was like "is that it?".

Also the 'hacking experience' is far from realistic. But I guess it serves the point of letting people feel like they're a hacker.

I really want to like this game, but I couldn't. The music is good though, I think it's the only plus side.

TL;DR: Cool hacking-look UI, repetitive hacking routine, weak story

It's been a while since I've given a recommendation this whole-hearted. I'll be honest, I didn't even mean to play this game, I launched it by accident while trying to open Halo, but man am I glad that I did. Great game with a good story and in-game terminal activities, however it could use a refresh. It's kind of stuck in the 90's, but I loved it all the same. I didn't like all the MS Win homage within a Linux or Unix terminal game. It's a simple version of the rich Linux OS (or Unix) and it's tools as well as the network concept. Which is fine, however the breaking into systems kind of gets old after the third or forth try. You learn that you have to acquire the tool for the job (port) and that's it. You acquire tools as you go, and you "steal" tools as you progress, but it's really simple. It's great all the same, just needs a few adjustments and improvements.

I though you could sell all that data or exchange it for tools, so I kept some of it from the big jobs, I ended up with a tone of stuff in / and /home, never being able to do anything with it.

What the game misunderstands, but makes easy on the player is:
- Unix and Linux binary files don't end in exe and don't use PE format, they use ELF.
- braking firewalls and proxy (well VPN servers) is not that easy and doesn't require any memory on the client/hacker side
- tracing a hacker is done differently, one could kick a user from his machine but not trace him in that way or that fast
- buffer overflow is simplistic and unimaginative 
- the memory concept could've been done differently with memory updates, etc. I expected more, it's just there to make your work slower so the tracer could kick in.
- Unix commands are not uppercase, and are case sensitive (I know, I know, I'm pushing it)
- firewalls and proxys are just there to make you slower, no concept of network or network security

Other Cons:
- no vi (yeah, I kept tying it all the same, and wondered why it didn't work), you have to use cat, replace
- you cannot create folders, no mkdir, which is weird
- no vi so, text editing, you have to kind of use replace, which works for the mostpart
- no touch, so you cannot make new files
- no shell scripts (shell is just a different concept all together)
- /home/ doesn't have a user, AT ALL
- root is admin
- no concept of mount or a filesystem
- no killall command
- there are no routers (because the game acts like we are in the 90's, but there are software firewalls and proxys)
- no VPN concept within the proxy
- no ssh shelling to the other machines and attacking from that machine (override doesn't count, you still have your own IP)
- ssh is just there because
- there are no worms, viruses or rootkits
- forkbomb is just a hard reboot
- the trigger/trap is a waste, you just need it once and never again, you don't even have to have the shells open in the other parts of the game and in the DLC
- the music, although OK for the mostpart, it's a little to digital for me and I kind of require more tones, metal or rock would 
suffice
- there are a few good tracks which have melody inside
- the game hinders CPU extensively (I'm playing it on Linux and this shouldn't happen), it could use with some optimization. I didn't notice this until I minimized the game, or went to shell to do something and saw the CPU cores all at 100% all the while the game was suspended, which is strange. I don't know how it was written, but these things only happen with Javascript.
- the IRC logs are old and outdated, from bash.org
- why do we even have IRC without being able to log and hack it?
- hexclock just randomly changes color as the time ticks, instead of being able you use -s or -n, which don't do anything, to change the hex color yourself.
- not all the save files sync via cloud for me, so I could not enjoy it on different machines, and had to copy the save files manually
- you cannot change the layout of the theme, switch the windows around and change color, leaving you with unwanted colors and layout for most of the time
- DLC themes are better than the original game
- Honeypot theme (you know which server I'm talking about) is just the GOLD theme - which you can acquire before attacking that server
- you don't have to actually delete the logs, it's just so you can complete the job
- no world interaction whatsoever, feels like the machines you break in have no owner and have been sitting there for ages (only one or two cases are dangerous, if we include the DLC, you will actually have to remain unnoticed, rest of the time you can do whatever you like) 
- even though the story starts good, the plot kind of goes off into another corner
- the hacknet program does nothing, and is just there for the plots sake, or in reference to the actual game binary
- there is no concept of money, you just hack for the sake of it
- DLC starting requires research, you have to start it via in-game plot points (it's triggered after you end the game, but it's stated no where how to turn it on)

Pros
- everything else is pro, which is alot
- you can scan for other machines within the network
- the terminal only theme and the network nods make it a great visual pleasure (for us Linux users at least)
- there are secrets within the game
- there are some pieces of the game that will make you feel like you're in a movie
- there are some well though out scenarios - including the DLC
- iOS, or eOS is present, so mobile hacking is possible although very simple and dull
- mobile hacking, pacemaker hacking, other medical devices (although they use the same tool)
- server secrets
- secret servers :D
- great ending (and DLC continuation)
- Neo? - or did I make a mistake (you know what I mean)
- there are some text files or manual documentation for the tools
- you can hack your ISP provider as well
- you can hack almost anything, with a few machines left unbreakable, I won't spoil it
- DLC is really good, so get that too

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]

It kept me engaged until the end. The puzzles are pretty straightforward if you are following along.

A number of other reviewers have pointed out a few obvious flaws (i.e. requiring deletion of log records, though the game does not punish you for forgetting). One of the strands is only available if you destroy a server, despite the "Mantra.txt" early in the game stating we should "Create more than we destroy." Despite these, it is a fun game for a reasonable price.
